title: Absolution and penance
hook: I absolve you, and a small penance to begin the repair

segments.voice: Yesterday, contrition: sorry from love, not only fear. Your line was sorry, and resolved.

A hiker carries a heavy pack so long she forgets it's there. She just walks a little bent over. Then someone lifts it off her shoulders, and for a second she nearly floats. Some people who come out of confession after years away describe it like that. They sit in the pew afterward, a bit stunned, lighter. What happened in there came down to a few words spoken by a priest, and then a small job to do on the way out.
screen: `A PACK SHE FORGOT.` → `LIFTED OFF.` → `A FEW WORDS, AND A SMALL JOB.`

segments.voice: Absolution comes from the Latin absolvere, to loosen, to set free, to untie, the same root as absolute and solve. When the priest absolves, Catholics believe the knots are untied. After the penitent's act of contrition, he extends his hand over their head and prays a short prayer of absolution. It names God as the Father of mercies, who reconciled the world through the death and resurrection of his Son and sent the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. It ends with the words at the heart of the sacrament. In the old Latin form: Ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis, in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti. I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The penitent answers amen. Catholics believe every sin confessed with real sorrow is forgiven then and there, completely. Then comes the piece that's often misunderstood: the penance. The priest gives a small task, often a few prayers, sometimes an act of kindness, reading a passage, or making something right. It isn't payment. You can't buy forgiveness, and the Church says so. It's more like physical therapy after surgery. The sin is forgiven, but it has left some damage, in you and around you, and penance begins the repair. When you can, that means real repair: returning what was taken, fixing what was broken. Zacchaeus, the tax collector, shows it. In the Douay-Rheims, he tells Jesus: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have wronged any man of any thing, I restore him fourfold." Forgiven, and then sent out to mend.
screen: `ABSOLVERE: TO LOOSEN, TO UNTIE.` · `EGO TE ABSOLVO.` · `PENANCE ISN'T PAYMENT.` · `ZACCHAEUS RESTORES FOURFOLD.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN, THEN SENT.`

segments.voice: Think back over what you've looked at this week and find something you damaged, even a little: a trust, a friendship, a borrowed thing, a reputation you shaded in conversation. Choose one small, concrete act that would begin to fix it, a call, a correction, giving something back, something doable. If you pray, ask for help to do it well.
Absolution. From the Latin for untying. The priest's words of forgiveness, and after them, a small penance to begin the repair. Today's word.
Your line: forgiven, then sent. The knots are untied first; the repair comes after. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At the end of confession the priest extends his hand and says the words of absolution; the penitent answers amen and later does the penance he gave, often a few prayers or a small act of repair.

what it means: Catholics believe God truly forgives through the priest's words, and the penance that follows begins the repair.
what a scholar hears: absolvere, to loosen; the Latin formula ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis; the Church teaches restitution is owed where possible.

notes: The English formula of absolution is ICEL text (copyrighted); the prayer is described, not quoted. The Latin core 'Ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis, in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti' is given with an English gloss. Confirm the Latin.
Penance as repair, not payment; restitution where possible: CCC 1459–1460. Physical therapy image is the writer's. Confirm.
Etymology: absolvere, ab + solvere (to loosen); 'absolute' and 'solve' share the root. Confirm.
